content_voiceover: Hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin, or HPFH, is the benign end of the gamma globin regulation spectrum, and the single most important distinguishing feature for boards is right in the definition: increased HbF in adult life without relevant hematologic abnormalities, meaning these patients are truly asymptomatic, unlike delta beta thalassemia, which we just covered, where similarly elevated HbF comes with an actual chain imbalance and a thalassemic phenotype. The mechanism split is the second key point. Deletional HPFH involves larger deletions removing both the delta and beta globin genes, similar in location to delta beta thalassemia deletions, but critically these HPFH deletions spare both the G gamma and A gamma genes, allowing continued robust gamma chain, fetal hemoglobin, production that fully compensates, that is why there is no clinical abnormality, versus delta beta thalassemia where compensation is only partial. Non deletional HPFH instead involves single point mutations in the promoter regions of the gamma globin genes themselves, the diagram shows specific positions upstream of the transcription start site, disrupting or enhancing binding at conserved regulatory elements like the CACCC box, the CCAAT boxes, and the ATAAA box, and these mutations increase baseline gamma gene transcription in adult life instead of it silencing normally after the fetal to adult hemoglobin switch.
keypoints: HPFH = ↑HbF in adults with NO hematologic abnormality — key differentiator from δβ-thalassemia
Deletional type: removes δ and β genes but spares Gγ and Aγ → full compensation
Non-deletional type: point mutations in γ-globin promoter boxes (CACCC, CCAAT, ATAAA)
Clinically silent — an important benign mimic of elevated HbF states
keypoint_voiceover: The defining feature of HPFH is right there in the name, elevated HbF in adults, but with no relevant hematologic abnormality, and that is what separates it from delta beta thalassemia. Two mechanisms produce it. Deletional HPFH removes the delta and beta genes but spares the gamma genes, so gamma chain output fully compensates. Non deletional HPFH comes from point mutations in the gamma globin gene promoters, at conserved regulatory sites like the CACCC and CCAAT boxes, that keep gamma gene transcription switched on into adulthood. Clinically, remember HPFH as the benign mimic, it shows elevated HbF on hemoglobin electrophoresis, but the patient is otherwise hematologically normal.
